Text 1
Fiction generally claims to represent “reality” (this is known as representation or
mimesis) in some way; however, because any narrative is presented through the
symbols and codes of human meaning and communication systems, fiction cannot
represent reality directly, and different narratives and forms of narrative represent
different aspects of reality, and represent reality in different ways.
This awareness that fiction is not merely a window onto the real but a mode of
constructing meaning is central to literary study. Every element in a text—its plot,
characterisation, imagery, even punctuation—is an intentional act of
representation, shaped by cultural norms, ideological frameworks, and historical
contexts, Thus, fiction becomes a site where assumptions about reality can be
reinforced or dismantled. When we read fiction critically, we engage in the work
of decoding its symbolic architecture. We Whose reality is being
represented? Whose voices are privileged, and whose are silenced? What
ideologies underpin the narrative structure?
The literary world, then, is not only a reflection of the real world—it is a
reconstruction, a space where power, identity, and truth are negotiated through
narrative form. Critical reading recognises this complexity, treating fiction as an
epistemological act: a way of knowing, interpreting, and even remaking the
world. As readers, we must move beyond passive consumption and begin to
question the aesthetic and ethical implications of what we read. Fiction, far from
being mere escapism, becomes a critical lens through which we explore—and
complicate—our understanding of reality.
JOHN LYE
Extract from Critical Reading: A Guide

I remember the light is hot and gold, spilling across our faces. That daytime
sunshine has burnt our cheeks and foreheads, but now the sun is dying, cooling,
seeping like a wound across the skyline. Our three little bodies sweat. The air has
stayed thick: humid and unmoving.
Then the sprinklers erupt suddenly with a tired hiss. Crumbs of water scatter in
sharp rivulets against the red of the sky. They pelt down over us. Droplets are like
cold metal coins against our chests, dripping down our arms, from our fingertips.
Our laughter punctures the drowsy neighbourhood; the shrieks and hoots and
squeals skid between the eucalypts, through parched flower bushes, across the
road.
We dance as our skin slides against each other, slimy and soft, and I am aware
that I can feel it all.
Tam eight and outside myself, like the heat has shimmered the world into memory
and this moment of my life is as frail as a mirage. I can see my grandmother. She
sits next to my grandfather on their red-brick porch, both squinting into the sunset
as they supervise. I can see the grass underneath me, orange and scorched and
stinging the skin of my bare feet. It is softening under the sprinklers; the dirt that
nests the blades thickened to mud. My brother yelps as he extricates a small
prickle that has burrowed between two of his toes. I can hear this yelp and the
giggling of my sister and the sluggish moan of blowflies licking our sweat. I can
taste the aridity of December, of suburbia a year before the country drips officially
into drought. I can smell it, too: the trembling asphalt roads and wilting buildings.
my head back and extend my tongue and let sweet, grass-flavoured water run
down my throat.
I drink like it is forever and it feels like it is, this summer, all those summers; long
yellow days stretching into infinite orange nights that skip together into the length
of a heartbeat that is no time at all. I look up at the magpies, lined up on my
grandmother’s roof, croaking in silence with their dry, watchful eyes.
Maybe it started then. The vicious throb inside me. It was an awareness: of the
slipping over my skin, the passings. I clutched desperately with my fingers but
still it left me. Even at eight years old, there was such futility in all that water-
sprinkler joy. I understood. I knew.

Text 2 (continued)
For as long as I can remember, I have collected things. When I was younger, it
was more severe, ambient: old shoelaces, the envelopes of birthday cards, empty
toilet paper rolls. They cluttered my room and filled me with a strange,
claustrophobic grief, but it was better than the alternative: of memories being lost,
becoming irretrievable. It seemed I was afflicted with a blistering impulse to
preserve and document. It was an inability to release, or maybe to surrender. So I
attached meaning to peculiar pieces of junk and stored them all inside my
bedroom.
The walls of the childhood bedroom I still sleep in are blue. My parents painted
it for me: the colour of the ocean and of sleep and the sky and melancholy. By the
window, my wardrobe presses into itself with clothes: basketball singlets from
each team I have played in; winter and summer uniforms from both primary and
secondary school; two shirts I wore on grade five camp. At the bottom of the
cupboard, there is a shoebox fill of all my old phones and computers. On the other
side, there is an unstable, accumulating stack of retired basketballs, the leather
collapsing in on itself through lack of use. Under my bed, another box is filled
with to-do lists and unused diaries and obsolete calendars and flattened toothpaste
tubes and empty water bottles and cheap posters I am too old to have hanging on
my walls so have folded up along with other, smaller boxes containing even
smaller boxes. I cannot throw out any of it.
After I finished school, I chose the only career that could both indulge and
provoke the fear of forgetting: the writer. Sometimes I write so late into the
morning, I lose myself. There is no sensation in my body; it has leaked from me,
and I wonder absently at my realnes
SARAID TAYLOR
Extract from The Intricacy of Magpies
